q: Grand cru ground on the Corton hill is shared by more than one commune. Which set of communes holds it?
exp: Corton and Corton-Charlemagne wrap around the shoulder of the hill and cross both boundaries, which is why a Ladoix or Pernand grower can own grand cru without their village ever appearing on the bottle. It is also why those two village names are among the best value on the Cote de Beaune: the reputation went to the hill, not to them.

q: Of the five grand crus on the Montrachet hill, Montrachet itself and Batard-Montrachet cross the Puligny-Chassagne boundary. Which one lies wholly inside Chassagne-Montrachet?
exp: Criots sits at the southern foot of Batard, entirely in Chassagne. Chevalier-Montrachet and Bienvenues-Batard-Montrachet are the mirror case, both wholly inside Puligny, which is why Puligny is usually credited with the finer end of the hill.

q: Tucked in a valley behind the Montrachet hill, one village sells most of its vineyard at premier cru level and is the standard recommendation for white Burgundy that does not cost a fortune. Name it.
exp: En Remilly and Les Murgers des Dents de Chien run right up to the Chevalier-Montrachet boundary, and the wines from them are recognisably of the same slope. The village sits in a side valley off the main Cote, which is the whole reason it was never priced with its neighbours.

q: Past Santenay the Cote de Beaune runs out in one last appellation, created in 1989 from villages that had hyphenated a shared vineyard name onto their own. Name it.
accept: maranges in the cote de beaune
exp: Cheilly, Dezize and Sampigny had all appended les-Maranges to their names, and the appellation simply took the vineyard name and dropped the villages. The ground faces south rather than east here as the Cote swings round, and it is the last of the Cote d'Or before the Chalonnaise begins.

q: Red wine from a premier cru lying inside the commune of Meursault goes to market under the Volnay name instead. Name that climat.
exp: Meursault sells white and Volnay sells red, so the rules let the Pinot Noir grown at Santenots take the name that will move it. White from the same rows stays Meursault. It is the plainest case in Burgundy of an appellation following reputation rather than the map.

q: A guest asks why they cannot compare one producer's Clos de Tart against another's, the way they might with Clos de Vougeot. What is the answer?
opts: Clos de Tart is a brand rather than a delimited vineyard
Clos de Tart may only be sold as Morey-Saint-Denis
Clos de Tart is a monopole, held entire by a single owner
Clos de Tart is a premier cru, so no producer may print its name
exp: Cistercian nuns planted it in the twelfth century and it has never been divided, so there is exactly one wine to taste in any vintage. Clos de Vougeot is the opposite case: one wall around ground that slopes from the road to the top of the hill, split among dozens of owners who each make something different from it.

q: Bressandes, Clos du Roi and Renardes appear on labels appended to a single grand cru name. Which grand cru takes them?
exp: Corton covers a long sweep of hillside, so the decree lets a grower add the climat to the grand cru name and say where on the hill the fruit grew. Gevrey works the other way round: each of its climats is an appellation in its own right, so Charmes-Chambertin is a name rather than a qualification of Chambertin.

q: A white grand cru appellation on the Corton hill is almost never seen on a bottle, because everyone entitled to it prefers a better-known name. Name the unused appellation.
exp: It remains on the books, and every grower who could use it labels the wine Corton-Charlemagne instead, which the market recognises and pays for. The two appellations cover overlapping ground, so the choice costs nothing and the shorter name has simply died of neglect.

q: A Morey-Saint-Denis climat was reassembled from scattered parcels over decades and raised from premier cru to grand cru in 1981. Name it.
exp: The vineyard had been split among many hands after the Revolution and was patiently bought back into one piece, which is what made the case for promotion arguable at all. A tiny fragment stayed outside the reassembly, so the grand cru is very nearly but not quite a monopole.

q: Directly above the most famous monopole in Vosne lies a grand cru of well under a hectare, the smallest appellation in France. Name it.
exp: It is a strip of slope no wider than a tennis court is long, and the whole appellation makes a few hundred cases in a generous year. Answering Romanee-Conti here is the standard error: that is the vineyard immediately below, and it is more than twice the size.

q: Chablis growers spent the 1970s in a public fight over where the appellation's edge should fall. What were the rival criteria?
opts: Whether oak ageing should be compulsory at premier cru and above
Whether soil alone should qualify, or slope and exposure too
Whether machine harvesting should be permitted below the premier cru rank
Whether the river should form the eastern limit of all planting
exp: One camp held that the grey Kimmeridgian marl was the appellation and nothing else could be Chablis; the other argued that a well-sited slope on the younger Portlandian limestone above it ripens perfectly well. The expansionists largely won, which is why the planted area is a multiple of what it was and why the argument still surfaces whenever a poor vintage is discussed.

q: Every one of the seven Chablis grand cru climats shares a single slope with the premier cru Montee de Tonnerre. Which bank of the Serein is it on, and which way does it face?
opts: The left bank, facing due south
The right bank, facing due north
exp: The Serein runs northwest through the town, and the right bank carries the one continuous southwest-facing wall of hillside that holds all seven grand cru climats, with Montee de Tonnerre and Fourchaume continuing it. Left bank climats such as Vaillons and Montmains face the other way and give lighter, quicker wines.

q: Twenty kilometres from Chablis, a village appellation makes red from Pinot Noir with a permitted minority of a rare local grape. Which grape may it add?
exp: Irancy is the Yonne's red appellation, and Cesar is a dark, tannic relation of Pinot Noir grown essentially nowhere else. A little of it stiffens a Pinot picked at the northern limit of ripeness, and too much of it makes the wine hard, which is why the ceiling is low.

q: One Burgundian village appellation is planted to Sauvignon Blanc rather than Chardonnay, which is much of why it waited until 2003 for recognition. Name it.
exp: It sat as a VDQS for decades because the authorities were reluctant to grant an appellation to a grape with no Burgundian standing. The vineyard is on the same Kimmeridgian ground as Chablis, close enough that a grower may own rows of both.

q: A named parcel straddling Vaudesir and Les Preuses is treated as grand cru without being one of the seven climats. Name that parcel.
exp: It is a monopole whose name is older than the 1938 decree but does not appear in it, since that decree lists only the seven climats; grand cru standing was granted to the parcel separately at the turn of the 1950s, so the label carries Chablis Grand Cru and the parcel name rather than either of the two climats it lies across. Anyone reciting the seven climats and expecting to have named every grand cru bottling has missed it.

q: Chablis keeps a traditional cask of its own, smaller than the standard Burgundian barrel and still used there as a unit of account. Name it.
exp: The Chablis feuillette holds a hundred and thirty-two litres against the two hundred and twenty-eight of a Burgundian piece, and confusingly the Cote d'Or has a feuillette of its own at a hundred and fourteen. Crops and contracts in the Yonne are still quoted in them long after the wine went into tank.
